items.explanation: These lines are from Lord Byron's satirical poem The Vision of Judgment (1822), written in ottava rima under the pseudonym 'Quevedo Redivivus.' The poem mocks Poet Laureate Robert Southey's hagiographic A Vision of Judgement and satirizes the late King George III's entry into heaven.

items.stem:

'Is there any point to which you would wish to draw my attention ?'

'To the curious incident of the dog in the night-time.'

'The dog did nothing in the night-time.'

What was Sherlock Holmes' response ?

structured.lead:
Here's a famous exchange from Arthur Conan Doyle's Silver Blaze :
'Is there any point to which you would wish to draw my attention ?'
'To the curious incident of the dog in the night-time.'
'The dog did nothing in the night-time.'
What was Sherlock Holmes' response ?
structured.options_hint: Nothing ? Nothing at all ? Rather unbeli

options: Nothing ? Nothing at all ? Rather unbelievable
That sounds rather curious, don't you think ?
items.explanation: This famous exchange occurs in Arthur Conan Doyle's short story 'The Adventure of Silver Blaze' (1892). Sherlock Holmes deduces that the racehorse was stolen by someone the watchdog knew well—its trainer, John Straker—because the dog did not bark during the night.

items.title: Q8 · Dec 2014 (Paper III)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Who among Shakespeare's contemporaries did not write tragedies ?

structured.lead: Who among Shakespeare's contemporaries did not write tragedies ?
structured.options_hint: Thomas Kyd John Lyly Christopher Marlowe

items.explanation: John Lyly was known exclusively for his Euphuistic prose romances and allegorical court comedies (such as Campaspe, Endymion, and Gallathea) rather than tragedies. In contrast, Thomas Kyd (The Spanish Tragedy), Christopher Marlowe (Doctor Faustus), and Ben Jonson (Sejanus, Catiline) all wrote tragedies.

items.title: Q11 · Dec 2014 (Paper III)
items.meta: Classical Greece (Attic Age) · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · Plato
items.stem: The issue of privileging speech over writing was taken up for discussion in Plato's

structured.lead: The issue of privileging speech over writing was taken up for discussion in Plato's
structured.options_hint: Ion Republic Book III Republic Book X Ph

items.explanation: In Plato's dialogue Phaedrus, Socrates recounts the myth of the Egyptian god Theuth (inventing writing) and King Thamus, arguing that writing is an inferior, lifeless reminder compared to living speech. Jacques Derrida famously deconstructs this logocentric hierarchy in 'Plato's Pharmacy' (1968).

structured.lead: The first major report on The Teaching of English in England was published in 1921. It is known as ________, named after the Chair, Board of Education, _______
structured.options_hint: Newbolt Report; Sir Henry Newbolt Wood's

options: Wood's Despatch; Charles Wood, Lord Halifax
items.explanation: In 1919, the British Board of Education appointed a Departmental Committee chaired by the poet Sir Henry Newbolt. Its landmark 1921 report, The Teaching of English in England (known as the Newbolt Report), established English literature and language as the central unifying core of national education.

items.title: Q15 · Dec 2014 (Paper III)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Who first developed the notion of 'competence' in language studies ?

structured.lead: Who first developed the notion of 'competence' in language studies ?
structured.options_hint: Dell Hymes Noam Chomsky Leech and Svartv

items.explanation: In Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965), Noam Chomsky introduced the fundamental distinction between linguistic 'competence' (an idealized speaker-hearer's internal, tacit knowledge of grammatical rules) and 'performance' (the actual use of language in concrete situations), extending Saussure's langue/parole dichotomy.

structured.lead:
The fruit was eaten.
The fruit is ripening.
Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct ?
(1)
English has two kinds of participle : the present and the past.
(2)
English has three kinds of participle : the present, the past and the future.
(3)
The first sentence here is an example of a verb in past participle.
(4)
The first sentence here is an example of a verb in the perfect tense.
(5)
The second sentence here is an example of a verb in present participle.
(6)
The second sentence here is an example of a verb in the continuous tense
structured.options_hint: 2, 4, 6 are correct 1, 5, 6 are correct

items.explanation: Statements 1, 3, and 5 are grammatically correct: English verbs form two participles—the present participle ending in -ing (such as 'ripening' in 'two ripening mangoes') and the past participle (such as 'eaten' in 'he has eaten').

items.title: Q20 · Dec 2014 (Paper III)

items.stem: 'Homonyms' are words that _______

structured.lead: 'Homonyms' are words that _______
structured.options_hint: are pronounced differently but have the

options: are pronounced differently but have the same meaning
refer to both the male and female of the human species
are spelt similarly but have different meanings
refer to people who live in houses with similar structures
items.explanation: Homographs (literally 'same writing') are words that share the exact same spelling but have different meanings and origins, and may or may not have different pronunciations—such as 'lead' (the metal) and 'lead' (to guide), or 'bank' (financial institution vs. river edge).

items.explanation: All four items belong to the Pre-Raphaelite movement: William Morris's poem The Earthly Paradise (1868–1870), Dante Gabriel Rossetti's translations Dante and His Circle (1861/1874), Christina Rossetti's Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862), and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood's short-lived periodical The Germ (1850).

items.title: Q72 · Dec 2014 (Paper III)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit II: Poetry · Emily Dickinson
items.stem:
Read the following poem and answer the question :

A Bird came down the Walk —
He did not know I saw —
He bit an Angleworm in halves
And ate the fellow, raw,

And then he drank a Dew
From a convenient Grass —
And then hopped sidewise to the Wall
To let a Beetle pass —

He glanced with rapid eyes
That hurried all around —
They looked like frightened Beads, I thought —
He stirred his Velvet Head

Like one in danger, Cautious,
I offered him a Crumb
And he unrolled his feathers
And rowed him softer home —

Than Oars divide the Ocean,
Too silver for a seam —
Or Butterflies, off Banks of Noon
Leap, plashless as they swim.

Is "a convenient Grass" an example of "transferred epithet" ?

structured.options_hint: Yes, it is. The "convenience" of grass i

options: Yes, it is. The "convenience" of grass is transferred from the bird to the poet who finds grass convenient of access

items.explanation: In Emily Dickinson's poem 'A Bird came down the Walk' (1862), the phrase 'a convenient Grass' is a classic example of a transferred epithet (hypallage): the adjective 'convenient' logically describes the bird's easy access rather than an inherent quality of the blade of grass itself.

items.explanation: In Dickinson's 'A Bird came down the Walk,' 'hopped,' 'hurried,' and 'glanced' are all dynamic kinetic images depicting the bird's physical movements, whereas 'his Velvet Head' is a tactile and visual metaphor describing the soft texture of its feathers.

items.explanation: Emily Dickinson's 'A Bird came down the Walk' dramatizes the quiet boundary and unbridgeable distance between the human observer (who cautiously offers a crumb) and the autonomous non-human world of nature (the bird that rejects the domestic offering and flies seamlessly away).
